title: Reading a written cleaning procedure and closing out the task
audience: Cleaners and team leads who must work from a written cleaning procedure and need to find the purpose, standard, hazard controls, timing guide and steps quickly and in the right order.
learningOutcomes: Locate the purpose, the finished standard, the hazard controls, the timing guide and the steps in a written cleaning procedure.
Explain why a timing guide is a planning aid and not a target to be used without checking it against the site.
Complete the close-out routine in the right order: equipment, storage, PPE, hand hygiene and the job record.

instruction.heading: How a usable cleaning procedure is laid out
instruction.body: A clear cleaning procedure does five things in a fixed order. It states the purpose of the task. It sets a required standard, which is the finished result you must reach. It lists the equipment and the hazards, with a control for each hazard. It gives an indicative time. Then it sets out numbered steps. A worker who knows where each of these sits can check any step in seconds, and can tell at a glance whether a procedure is complete.

instruction.heading: Read the standard before the steps
instruction.body: The steps are only a route to the standard. Before you pick up a cloth or a mop, read what finished looks like for that surface, such as dust-free, streak-free or an even sheen. If a finish is damaged, the standard may not be reachable with the method in the procedure. That is a fault to report, not a reason to work harder with the same method.

instruction.heading: Treat the hazard controls as a checklist
instruction.body: The hazard table tells you what to control before you start: slips and falls, manual handling, electrical equipment, chemical use and the rest. The controls it lists are minimum controls. Where the site's approved procedure or the state or territory rule is stricter, follow the stricter one. Tick off each control you have applied before you begin the numbered steps.

instruction.heading: Timing guides are planning aids
instruction.body: A procedure may give an indicative time for an area. Use it as a rough guide for planning only. It assumes conditions that may not be present, such as clear floors, light soil or easy access. Your business should measure its own rates on its own surfaces before it quotes or schedules work, and should record the actual time taken. The timing figures in the source document are unverified and are not Australian benchmarks, so this lesson does not use them.

instruction.heading: Close-out is part of the job
instruction.body: The last steps are not optional tidying. Put equipment away, clean the tools, store cords, pads and brushes in the designated place, remove PPE, perform hand hygiene and record the job. An incomplete close-out is how the next job starts with dirty or damaged tools, and how a fault goes unreported.

procedure: Locate the purpose, the required standard and the equipment list before you start.
Read the hazard and control table and tick each control you will apply.
Confirm that the written steps match the site's approved procedure, and note any stricter site rule.
Get the kit and PPE ready, and check each item for damage and inspection status.
Work through the numbered steps in order. If a step cannot be done as written, stop and ask the team leader.
Check the finished area against the required standard, not against the number of steps you completed.
Clean and return all equipment, and store cords and pads as the procedure states.
Remove PPE, perform hand hygiene and complete the job record, noting the procedure version used.

workedExamples.situation: You are given a one-page procedure for a hard floor. One step says to wet mop with an approved detergent, but the detergent named is not on the site's approved product list.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you use the nearest product you have?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Stop and ask the team leader which product is approved for the site. The procedure names a method, and the product must come from the site's approved list and be used as its label directs. Note the query on the job record so the procedure can be corrected.

workedExamples.situation: The timing guide suggests a set time for a 100 square metre area. The room is full of furniture that must be moved, and the floor is heavily soiled.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you hold the guide's time?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The guide assumes conditions that are not present. Plan the extra time for moving furniture and removing heavy soil, and record the actual time taken so the business can build its own rate.

equipmentAndPpe: The written procedure for the task, at its current version
The site's list of approved products, with safety data sheets available
Task-specific PPE, as the procedure and the site rules specify
Equipment listed in the procedure, inspected before use

commonErrors.error: Working to the number of steps and ignoring the required standard.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the finish against the required standard before you sign the area off.

commonErrors.error: Using a product that is not on the approved list because it looks similar.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop and check the approved list and the label before the product is used.

commonErrors.error: Skipping close-out because the job is nearly finished.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat close-out as part of the task, and use the completion checklist every time.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Hazard controls in a written procedure are minimum controls. Where a state or territory WHS requirement or the site's procedure is stricter, follow the stricter requirement.

The reference document (one module of a cleaning procedure set, version 1, dated July 2012) does not name the issuing organisation. Its timings and its equipment references are not used for Australian work until checked.
Completing this lesson does not qualify a cleaner for any task that needs a licence or authorisation.

qualityStandard: The required standard and the hazard controls are identified before work starts.
The site's approved product list is checked before any product is used.
The finished area is checked against the required standard.
documentationEvidence: Completed job record showing the procedure version used
Notes on any step that could not be completed as written, and who was told
summary: A procedure has a purpose, a standard, hazard controls, a timing guide and steps, in that order.
The standard is the finish you are aiming for; the steps are the route to it.
Timing guides are planning aids, and close-out is part of the job.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which part of a written procedure tells you what a finished area should look like?
A procedure names a method, but the product it names is not on the site's approved list. What should you do?
options: Use the closest product you have, since it should work on the same surface.
Stop and ask the team leader for the approved product before using anything.
Use the product now and record it afterwards once the job is done.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a timing guide be treated as a planning aid?
options: It is a legally binding target for every job, and it must be met exactly regardless of site conditions.
It assumes conditions that may not exist on a given site, so the business should measure its own rates.
It is accurate for every site, so the business can price from it directly and it needs no further checking.
